---
title: "The Wall Street Journal chart style, 2010 to 2014"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
## ragg writes plain sRGB PNGs; the macOS default device embeds a profile that darkens colors.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", dpi = 192, dev = "ragg_png", fig.width = 3.4, fig.height = 4.2)
## Fold each chunk's code behind a "Code" toggle; output stays visible.
local({
  source_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
  knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
    paste0("\n\n<details><summary>Code</summary>\n\n", source_hook(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
  })
})
```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
## The chart records, the citation helpers and the drawing helpers.
source("wsj-guide.R")
set.seed(2012)
n_all <- nrow(charts)
n_read <- nrow(read)
axis_charts <- read[read$y_axis_side != "none", ]
## The first chart with the credit line on each desk, and the charts after it.
credit_from <- tapply(read$date[read$credit == "True"], read$desks[read$credit == "True"], min)
# The prose says the credit line arrived on both groups of desks on one day.
stopifnot(length(unique(credit_from)) == 1)
after_credit <- read[read$date >= credit_from[[1]], ]
us_white <- charts$desks == "US" & charts$field == "white" & charts$period %in% c("B", "C")
## The median darkness of the gray subtitles from September 2013 on, on each group of desks.
ink_median <- function(desks) {
  g <- charts[charts$gray_text == "True" & charts$desks == desks & charts$date >= "2013-09-01", ]
  round(median(as.numeric(g$subtitle_ink), na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

The *Wall Street Journal* published a book on its chart style in 2010, Dona Wong's *The Wall Street Journal Guide to Information Graphics*, but the book teaches judgment. It gives no colors and no measurements.
This article describes the charts themselves, as they ran on the paper's website from late 2010 to mid-2014, and shows how to draw them with `theme_wsj()` and the other WSJ tools in ggthemes.
`theme_wsj()` draws the charts of mid-2012 to mid-2013 by default, and its arguments set the other periods; the [recipe at the end](#with-ggthemes) puts the pieces together.

It is based on `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")` charts, the "native size" graphics that ran beside articles on the paper's website, dated `r format(min(as.Date(charts$date)), "%B %Y")` to `r format(max(as.Date(charts$date)), "%B %Y")`.
`r nrow(asia)` come from the *Journal*'s Asia desks: `r sum(charts$desk == "AI")` from the Asia news pages and `r sum(charts$desk == "AM")` from the Asian markets pages.
The other `r format(sum(charts$desks == "US"), big.mark = ",")` come from the U.S. desks, the web versions of print graphics: `r sum(charts$desk == "P1")` from page one, `r sum(charts$desk == "NA")` from the U.S. news pages and `r sum(charts$desk == "MK")` from Marketplace.
The archive has none from 2015: searches for later graphics returned only re-captures of older ones.
The colors and the type of every chart were measured from its pixels. Every Asia chart was also read, all but two of them twice; the U.S. charts were read once, in a sample of `r nrow(us_read)` drawn from each desk and half-year in proportion to its size.
So shares of what the pixels show are of all `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")` charts, and shares of what the readings recorded are of the `r n_read` charts read. Where the two groups of desks differ, both are given.
Shares come with their counts, as in "62%, 140 of 226 charts".
Each rule links to examples, and each chart cited was checked by eye. The link goes to the archived image.
No WSJ images are reproduced here. The figures are *ggplot2* drawings: most use made-up data, and a few copy the numbers of the chart they follow.
How the evidence was gathered is described [at the end](#how-this-guide-was-made).

## Four periods

The style changed three times in four years, on both groups of desks at once, so this guide splits the charts into four periods.

```{r period-table, echo = FALSE}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(charts, charts$period), function(d) {
  r <- d[d$read == "True", ]
  a <- d[d$desks == "Asia", ]
  data.frame(
    Period = d$period[1],
    Dates = periods$dates[periods$period == d$period[1]],
    Charts = nrow(d),
    Read = nrow(r),
    Field = paste(names(sort(table(d$field), decreasing = TRUE))[1:2], collapse = ", "),
    `Slab-serif title` = pct(r$title_typeface == "slab_serif", nrow(r)),
    `Bold subtitle` = pct(a$subtitle_weight == "bold", sum(a$subtitle_weight != "")),
    Bands = pct(r$rules == "bands", nrow(r)),
    `Credit line` = pct(r$credit == "True", nrow(r)),
    `Gray type` = pct(d$gray_text == "True", nrow(d)),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(
  tab,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste(
    "The field and the gray type were measured on every chart; the title, the bands and the credit line are from the",
    "charts read, and the subtitle weight from the Asia charts only",
    "(see [How this guide was made](#how-this-guide-was-made))."
  )
)
```

- **A, to September 2011.** A white or pale blue field, a plain sans-serif title over a bold subtitle, and bright, pure colors. No "The Wall Street Journal" credit line. The U.S. desks used a full bright set, royal blue `r wsj_col("royal blue")` before all, then red `r wsj_col("bright red")`, green `r wsj_col("bright green")`, black and yellow (see [Period A's bright set](#period-as-bright-set)); the few Asia charts of the period use almost only the red and the green. `r pct(charts$period == "A" & charts$desks == "US" & charts$field == "white", charts$period == "A" & charts$desks == "US")` of the U.S. charts are on white. Some charts mark their scale with bands, `r by_desk(read[read$period == "A", ], rules == "bands")`. On `r sum(asia$period == "A" & asia$field == "blue" & !is.na(asia$title_ink) & asia$title_ink >= 15)` of the `r sum(asia$period == "A" & asia$field == "blue")` pale blue Asia charts all the type, title included, is a near-black gray rather than black. Examples: `r cite(c("MK-BL067_SOUTHW_NS_20110404181215.jpg", "P1-BB372A_TRADE_NS_20110628174503.jpg", "AI-BG392_QE2REA_NS_20101104140201.jpg", "AI-BH794_BOK_NS_20110112225403.jpg"))`.
- **B, October 2011 to June 2012.** The redesign: an ivory field, a heavy slab-serif title and the muted palette of the rest of this guide. The credit line under the source follows three months later, on the same day on both groups of desks, 16 January 2012. The subtitle is still bold. Some charts mark their scale with alternating bands rather than dotted rules, `r by_desk(read[read$period == "B", ], rules == "bands")`. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-BN971_JECON_NS_20111010233303.jpg", "AI-BQ436_SKECON_NS_20120201013603.jpg", "AI-BR349_JECON_NS_20120311232103.jpg"))`.
- **C, July 2012 to July 2013.** As B, but the subtitle is set in regular weight, and bands fade out after 2012. On the U.S. desks the gray field of period D comes in early, still with black type: `r share(charts$period == "C" & charts$desks == "US" & charts$field == "gray", charts$period == "C" & charts$desks == "US")`, against `r pct(asia$period == "C" & asia$field == "gray", asia$period == "C")` on the Asia desks. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-BU349_SPAIN_NS_20120719113903.jpg", "AI-BW723_JECON_NS_20121030003018.jpg", "AI-BY469_CINVES_NS_20130116122703.jpg"))`; on gray, `r cite(c("NA-BS871_CHEAPD_NS_20121007170903.jpg", "MK-CD521_SELFIN_NS_20130527183303.jpg"))`.
- **D, from August 2013.** The field turns pale gray, and the subtitle, axis labels, notes, and source turn dark gray, about `#444444`; the title stays black. The gray type comes in in July 2013 and is on most charts from September. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-CC842A_APURS_NS_20130813000004.jpg", "AI-CC875_ARATES_NS_20130814225706.jpg", "AI-CF534_BITCOI_NS_20131218055104.jpg", "MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg"))`.

`theme_wsj()` draws period C by default and period D, gray type included, with `paper = "gray"`. Period B is `subtitle_face = "bold"`, and for its charts with bands, `rules = "none"` with `wsj_bands()`; period A adds `paper = "pale_blue"` or `"white"`, a sans title and a plain title weight.
The same made-up chart in each period's style, left to right A to D:

```{r period-examples, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(1)
## One chart, four looks. period_plot() in wsj-guide.R adds the bands of A and B and each period's overrides of
## theme_wsj().
d <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("2010-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 21))
d$value <- round(pmin(2400, pmax(250, 1200 + cumsum(stats::rnorm(21, -20, 260)))))
base <- function(fill, title = "Current Account", credit = TRUE) {
  ggplot(d, aes(date, value)) +
    geom_col(fill = fill, width = 24) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2010-01-01", "2011-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(prefix = "¥"), breaks = seq(0, 2500, 500), limits = c(0, 2500),
                       expand = expansion(0)) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      subtitle = "Japan’s current account,\nin billions of yen",
      caption = paste0("Source: Ministry of Finance", if (credit) "\nThe Wall Street Journal")
    )
}
side_by_side(list(
  ## A: a sans title, bright colors, no credit line.
  period_plot(base(wsj_col("bright red"), credit = FALSE), "A"),
  period_plot(base(wsj_col("steel")), "B"),
  period_plot(base(wsj_col("steel")), "C"),
  period_plot(base(wsj_col("steel")), "D")
))
```

Period A follows `r cite(c("AI-BG392_QE2REA_NS_20101104140201.jpg", "AI-BH794_BOK_NS_20110112225403.jpg"))`; period B, `r cite("AI-BN971_JECON_NS_20111010233303.jpg")`, whose unit and scale this chart borrows.

### Type

The charts set their titles in a heavy Ionic slab serif and everything else in a narrow sans.
The *Journal*'s own faces of these years were [Exchange](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/exchange-merges-historical-strategies-to-find-its-own-voice/), an Ionic slab that Tobias Frere-Jones designed as the paper's text face and that it adopted in 2007, and [Retina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina_(typeface)), his narrow sans for the stock tables.
The titles and labels in the corpus look like them, but no source found says which faces the graphics desk used.
Both are commercial. The nearest free faces, both on Google Fonts, are:

- **Titles:** [Bitter](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Bitter) in its heaviest weight. Roboto Slab Black is close but wider; Rockwell, where installed, is a geometric slab and reads rounder than the original.
- **Subtitles, labels, and sources:** [Source Sans 3](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Source+Sans+3), semibold for the bold subtitles of periods A and B. Fira Sans Condensed is narrower than the original.
- **Period A titles:** Source Sans 3 semibold, the same sans as the labels.

`theme_wsj()` takes them through `title_family` and `base_family`. The *systemfonts* package can fetch them from Google Fonts, and the heavy weight needs a name of its own:

```{r fonts, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
systemfonts::require_font("Bitter")
systemfonts::require_font("Source Sans 3")
systemfonts::register_variant("Bitter Heavy", "Bitter", weight = "heavy")
p + theme_wsj(base_family = "Source Sans 3", title_family = "Bitter Heavy")
```

The figures in this guide use these faces when they can be fetched, and the generic serif and sans when they cannot.

**Ink.** Until mid-2013 all the type is black. From July 2013 everything but the title is a dark gray: the subtitle, the axis labels, the notes and source, and the credit line all change, and the title does not. The change shows in the darkest pixels of the subtitle, on a scale where 0 is black and 255 white: black subtitles measure close to 0, and gray ones about `r ink_median("Asia")` on the Asia charts and `r ink_median("US")` on the U.S. charts, whose type measures darker though by eye it is the same gray. Small type never reaches the full value of its ink, so these levels show that the ink changed, not what it became. `theme_wsj()` uses `#444444`, an estimate rather than a measurement. Of the charts from September 2013 on, `r by_desk(charts[charts$date >= "2013-09-01", ], gray_text == "True")` have gray type; the measurement counts all of them, read or not. Compare the black type of `r cite("AI-CB568_AUSJOB_NS_20130613041804.jpg")` with `r cite(c("AI-CC875_ARATES_NS_20130814225706.jpg", "AI-CG344_INDIAR_NS_20140128030303.jpg"))`. The U.S. charts make the same change, `r cite(c("MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg", "MK-CJ995_TWITTE_NS_20140210182103.jpg"))`.
`theme_wsj(paper = "gray")` sets the gray type with the gray field. On another field, set it with `ink = "gray"`, and keep black type on gray with `ink = "black"`, as the U.S. desks did in period C.

```{r periods, fig.width = 5.2, fig.height = 4}
## Shares of the charts by half-year: the fields of all charts, the bands of the charts read, and the subtitle weight
## of the Asia charts.
charts$half <- paste0(substr(charts$date, 1, 4), ifelse(as.integer(substr(charts$date, 6, 7)) <= 6, "-03-31", "-09-30"))
halves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(charts, charts$half), function(d) {
  r <- d[d$read == "True", ]
  a <- r[r$desks == "Asia" & r$subtitle_weight != "", ]
  data.frame(
    half = as.Date(d$half[1]),
    what = c("Ivory field", "Gray field", "Bands", "Bold subtitle"),
    share = c(
      mean(d$field == "ivory"),
      mean(d$field == "gray"),
      mean(r$rules == "bands"),
      mean(a$subtitle_weight == "bold")
    ),
    n = c(nrow(d), nrow(d), nrow(r), nrow(a))
  )
}))
## Leave out a half-year with too few charts for a share, such as the second half of 2014.
halves <- halves[halves$n >= 10, ]
ends <- halves[halves$half == max(halves$half), ]
ggplot(halves, aes(half, 100 * share, colour = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date(c("2012-03-31", "2013-12-15", "2012-09-30", "2011-03-31")),
    y = c(95, 60, 28, 92),
    label = c("Ivory field", "Gray field", "Bands", "Bold subtitle"),
    colour = c(wsj_col("gold"), "#000000", wsj_col("steel"), wsj_col("red")),
    hjust = c(0.5, 0, 0, 0),
    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`Ivory field` = wsj_col("gold"), `Gray field` = "#000000", Bands = wsj_col("steel"),
               `Bold subtitle` = wsj_col("red")),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(2011:2014, "-01-01")),
    labels = wsj_year_label(),
    minor_breaks = as.Date(paste0(2010:2014, "-07-01")),
    ## Reach back to January 2011, so the first year is labeled.
    limits = as.Date(c("2011-01-01", NA)),
    guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25), limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Changing Looks",
    subtitle = "Share of charts in each half-year with each feature",
    caption = paste0("Note: Bold subtitles of Asia charts only\nSource: ", format(n_all, big.mark = ","),
                     " WSJ web graphics, measured and read for this guide")
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

## The parts of a chart

Every chart has the same parts, top to bottom.

1. **A title.** A short headline in a heavy slab serif, in title case: `r pct(lengths(strsplit(read$title, " +")) == 2, n_read)` of titles are two words and `r pct(lengths(strsplit(read$title, " +")) <= 3, n_read)` three or fewer. The longer ones are mostly on the U.S. desks, where a page-one chart may have only a sentence for a headline: `r cite(c("P1-BC563_VITALS_NS_20110919123602.jpg", "P1-BI200_VITALS_NS_20120920162703.jpg"))`. Some name the subject plainly (*South Korea's GDP*, *Japan's Trade Balance*), others make a point (*Slowing Down*, *Danger Zone*, *Hot Property*).
2. **A subtitle.** It says what is measured and in what unit, in plain words: "Change from previous quarter, seasonally adjusted"; "Japan's trade balance, in trillions of yen". `r share(read$subtitle != "", n_read, "charts read")` have one. Some add a sentence of news before the measure, a few on the Asia desks, mostly in periods C and D, and many more on the U.S. desks: `r cite(c("AM-BB585_CHINAH_NS_20131223060011.jpg", "AI-CF534_BITCOI_NS_20131218055104.jpg", "MK-CD521_SELFIN_NS_20130527183303.jpg"))`.
3. **The chart.** No axis titles: the subtitle has already given the unit, and the topmost y label repeats its symbol.
4. **Notes and sources**, small, at the bottom left: "Note:" first, then "Source:" or "Sources:" (`r share(read$has_source == "True", n_read, "charts read")`). Footnotes are marked with an asterisk in the chart and explained in the note.
5. **A credit line**, "The Wall Street Journal", on its own line under the source. It is not part of the redesign of October 2011: none of the `r sum(read$period == "B" & read$date < min(credit_from))` charts read from then to mid-January 2012 has it. It first appears on `r format(as.Date(credit_from[[1]]), "%e %B %Y")` on both groups of desks, `r cite("AI-BQ125_CECON_NS_20120116223902.jpg")`, and from that day on it is on `r by_desk(after_credit, credit == "True")`; the U.S. charts without it are mostly from 2012: `r cite(c("MK-BR882A_NETFL_NS_20120125183903.jpg", "MK-BU217_CISCO_NS_20120509181212.jpg"))`. Without it: `r cite(c("AI-BO366_SKECON_NS_20111027030302.jpg", "AI-BQ033_JECON_NS_20120111230006.jpg"))`.

```{r anatomy}
## Each chart of made-up data sets its own seed, so that adding a chart does not change the others.
set.seed(2012)
## Monthly change, with gains in green and losses in red and a black callout on the latest value.
d <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("2011-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 22))
d$value <- round(stats::rnorm(22, 0.4, 2.6), 1)
d$value[22] <- -4.1
## Name the levels in the palette's order, gains first, so gains take its first color.
d$sign <- factor(ifelse(d$value >= 0, "positive", "negative"), levels = c("positive", "negative"))
ggplot(d, aes(date, value, fill = sign)) +
  geom_col(width = 25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  wsj_callout(d$date[22], -4.1, "Oct.\n-4.1%", nudge_x = -30, nudge_y = -10, size = 3, family = wsj_text_font) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  scale_fill_wsj("direction", guide = "none") +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2011-01-01", "2012-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label(),
               minor_breaks = d$date, guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%", accuracy = 0.1), breaks = seq(-7.5, 5, 2.5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Factory Slump",
    subtitle = "Industrial production, change from\nprevious month",
    caption = "Note: Seasonally adjusted\nSource: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

The chart above follows `r cite("AI-BW723_JECON_NS_20121030003018.jpg")`.

## The field and the scale

**The field** is a flat color behind the whole graphic, title and source included, not just the plot.
Its colors were measured on every chart:

- ivory, `#f8f2e4`, on `r share(charts$field == "ivory" & charts$period %in% c("B", "C"), sum(charts$period %in% c("B", "C")))` in periods B and C;
- pale gray, `#efefef`, on `r share(charts$field == "gray" & charts$period == "D", sum(charts$period == "D"))` in period D;
- white or a pale blue, `#eff4f9`, in period A. The U.S. desks kept the pale blue for some charts after the redesign, `r share(charts$desks == "US" & charts$field == "blue" & charts$period %in% c("B", "C"), charts$desks == "US" & charts$period %in% c("B", "C"))` in periods B and C: `r cite(c("MK-BX810_SODA_NS_20121008174503.jpg", "MK-CB777B_TIFFA_NS_20130320203604.jpg"))`. They kept white for as many, `r share(us_white, charts$desks == "US" & charts$period %in% c("B", "C"))`, `r sum(us_white & grepl("VITALS", charts$file))` of them the page-one "Vitals" charts: `r cite(c("P1-BM308_VITALS_NS_20130715170308.jpg", "MK-BQ740_TIME_NS_20111130180903.jpg"))`;
- a pale green, `#f2f9f2`, on the Asia desks kept for one recurring chart, the HSBC purchasing managers' index for China, with its "Expanding" and "Contracting" scale bar: `r cite(c("AI-BP465_CHINAP_NS_20111215010903.jpg", "AI-BV767_CECON_NS_20120919230902.jpg"))`. The U.S. desks used it now and then for any chart: `r cite(c("NA-BT565_CASINO_NS_20121109182411.jpg", "P1-BK111_ECONOM_NS_20130130175403.jpg"))`.

The measured field colors are the same on both groups of desks. Each is a `paper` of `theme_wsj()`: `"ivory"`, `"gray"`, `"pale_blue"`, `"white"` and `"pale_green"`.

**The scale** is marked by thin horizontal dotted rules (`r share(read$rules == "dotted", n_read, "charts read")`) or, mostly in 2011 and 2012, by alternating bands of a darker tint of the field (in periods A to C, `r by_desk(read[read$period != "D", ], rules == "bands")`; `r sum(read$rules == "bands" & read$period == "D")` charts after). Some U.S. charts use thin solid rules instead (`r sum(us_read$rules == "solid")` read), among them the page-one "Vitals" charts: `r cite(c("P1-BC563_VITALS_NS_20110919123602.jpg", "P1-BI200_VITALS_NS_20120920162703.jpg"))`. The solid rules are a darker gray than the dotted ones, `#6d6d6d`, measured on the rules that fall on a single pixel row. `theme_wsj()` draws dotted rules, solid rules with `rules = "solid"`, and none with `rules = "none"`, for bands. The band on ivory measures `#efe4c9`; on gray, `#dddddd`; on pale blue, `#d7e4ee`. `wsj_bands()` takes the field and draws them. Shading starts with the interval above the lowest break and alternates up.
There are no vertical rules.
Bands: `r cite(c("AI-BN971_JECON_NS_20111010233303.jpg", "AI-BR349_JECON_NS_20120311232103.jpg", "AI-BS569_INDIIR_NS_20120502083603.jpg"))`. Dotted rules: `r cite(c("AI-BQ436_SKECON_NS_20120201013603.jpg", "AI-BT650_JECON_NS_20120620002102.jpg", "AI-CC875_ARATES_NS_20130814225706.jpg"))`.

**A solid black line** runs along zero or along the bottom of the plot on `r share(axis_charts$baseline == "black_solid", nrow(axis_charts), "charts read with a value axis")`. It belongs to the data, so `theme_wsj()` leaves it to `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)`.

```{r field-bands}
set.seed(3)
d <- walk(30, 3, 0.6, 0.3)
p <- ggplot(d, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = wsj_col("steel"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(paste0(2011:2013, "-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(prefix = "$"), breaks = seq(0, 12, 2), limits = c(0, 12),
                     expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(
    title = "Steady Climb",
    subtitle = "Monthly exports, in billions of\nU.S. dollars",
    caption = wsj_caption("Ministry of Commerce")
  )
## Period B: bands, with a bold subtitle. The bands go first so they draw behind the line.
p_bands <- p
p_bands$layers <- c(wsj_bands(), p$layers)
p_bands +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font, subtitle_face = "bold", rules = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

```{r field-gray}
## Period D: the gray field and dotted rules.
p +
  theme_wsj(paper = "gray", base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

## Axes

- **Values on the left, aligned right.** The y labels sit on the left (`r share(axis_charts$y_axis_side %in% c("left", "both"), nrow(axis_charts), "charts read with a value axis")`), centered on their rule, with no tick. They are set flush right on their numbers, and the unit on the top label hangs outside the column: in "20%" over "15", the "20" sits above the "15" and the "%" sticks out toward the plot; in "\$120" over "100" the "\$" sticks out to the left. Of `r nrow(ylabel_check)` charts checked by eye, `r sum(ylabel_check$align == "right")` are aligned right, `r sum(ylabel_check$align == "undecided")` have labels all of one width and cannot tell, `r sum(ylabel_check$align == "other")` is irregular, and none is aligned left: `r cite(c("AI-CA928_CECON_NS_20130513065706.jpg", "AI-BY469_CINVES_NS_20130116122703.jpg", "AI-CF943_CEXPOR_NS_20140109221206.jpg"))`. `theme_wsj()` aligns them right, and `wsj_label()` hangs the suffix.

  On the Asia desks a right-hand axis appears only as the second axis of a two-scale chart (`r sum(read$y_axis_side == "both")` charts): `r cite(c("AI-BS851_CECON_NS_20120515142403.jpg", "AM-BA672_CHINAH_NS_20131014054803.jpg"))`, or on the right-hand panel of a pair: `r cite("AI-BW445A_SPAIN_NS_20121017130604.jpg")`. A few U.S. charts put their only axis on the right (`r sum(us_read$y_axis_side == "right")` read): `r cite(c("MK-BS563A_APPLE_NS_20120228180904.jpg", "MK-BY239_4PROFI_NS_20121024181510.jpg"))`.
- **The unit on the top label only.** "8%", then 6, 4, 2; "$250 billion", then 225, 200. Of the charts read whose axis carries a unit symbol, `r share(read$y_unit_top_only == "True", sum(read$y_unit_top_only %in% c("True", "False")))` put it on the top label alone: `r cite(c("AI-BU349_SPAIN_NS_20120719113903.jpg", "AI-BU867_Econom_NS_20120809135703.jpg", "AM-BB585_CHINAH_NS_20131223060011.jpg"))`. Use `wsj_label()`. A worded unit hangs like a symbol: "$250 billion" over "225".
- **Ticks under the x axis**, hanging down from the baseline (`r share(read$x_ticks == "below", sum(read$x_ticks != "none"), "charts read with x ticks")`): `r cite(c("AI-BQ436_SKECON_NS_20120201013603.jpg", "MK-BT730_MSOFT_NS_20120419183018.jpg"))`. Smaller ticks between them mark months or quarters, on `r by_desk(read, minor_ticks == "True")`: `r cite(c("AI-BW723_JECON_NS_20121030003018.jpg", "MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg"))`.
- **Years abbreviated.** The first year in full and the rest with an apostrophe, "2011 '12 '13", on `r share(read$year_labels %in% c("mixed", "abbreviated"), sum(read$year_labels %in% c("mixed", "abbreviated", "full")), "charts read labeled by year")`: `r cite(c("AI-BR349_JECON_NS_20120311232103.jpg", "MK-BW709_LIQUOR_NS_20120823175703.jpg"))`. Fiscal years start "FY2011": `r cite("MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg")`. Use `wsj_year_label()`.
- **Labels after the tick, or on the point.** The label after the tick is the commoner on the Asia desks, the centered label on the U.S. desks.

  Where the data are monthly or daily, the tick marks the start of the year and the label is set just to its right, so "'12" reads as the year that begins there: `r cite(c("AI-BQ436_SKECON_NS_20120201013603.jpg", "AI-BR349_JECON_NS_20120311232103.jpg", "MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg"))`. Use `theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))`. Where there is one value a year, the tick is on the value and the label is centered under it: `r cite(c("MK-BT552_EBOOKS_NS_20120412173602.jpg", "MK-BW709_LIQUOR_NS_20120823175703.jpg", "MK-BU489A_AMC_NS_20120521183610.jpg"))`. The label is after the tick on `r by_desk(read, x_label_position == "right_of_tick", x_label_position != "", "charts with x labels")`. Bars of categories, such as quarters, are labeled centered under each bar.
- **Inverted scales** are allowed and flagged. A currency chart may turn its axis over so that down means weaker, with a footnote saying so: `r cite("AM-AZ574_AMONEY_NS_20130724132404.jpg")`.

```{r axes}
set.seed(4)
d <- data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("2010-09-01"), by = "month", length.out = 40))
d$value <- 52 - 0.4 * seq_len(40) + 1.5 * sin(seq_len(40) / 2) + stats::rnorm(40, 0, 0.8)
ggplot(d, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = wsj_col("red"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(2011:2013, "-01-01")),
    labels = wsj_year_label(),
    minor_breaks = d$date,
    guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(30, 60, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Losing Ground",
    subtitle = "Share of exports going to Europe",
    caption = wsj_caption("Customs department")
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0), axis.minor.ticks.length.x = unit(1.5, "pt"))
```

## Color

### The palette

The colors below were measured from flat areas of the charts. They are the modal colors of each cluster across every chart that uses it, not estimates from one image.
The same values recur exactly from chart to chart, which suggests a fixed set of swatches.
Each hue comes in up to three shades.

```{r palette, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.6}
## The house colors from the redesign on; period A's bright set is drawn in its own section.
bright_inks <- c("bright red", "pale bright red", "royal blue", "pale royal blue", "bright green", "pale bright green",
                 "bright yellow")
pal <- inks[!inks$ink %in% c("blue", bright_inks), ]
## The lightest orange is not measured, so it has no count.
pale_orange <- data.frame(ink = "pale orange", hex = wsj_pal("oranges")(3)[3], A = NA, B = NA, C = NA, D = NA,
                           Asia = NA, US = NA, charts = NA)
pal <- rbind(pal[pal$ink != "gold" & pal$ink != "tan" & pal$ink != "pale gold" & pal$ink != "yellow" &
                   pal$ink != "black", ],
             pale_orange, pal[pal$ink %in% c("gold", "tan", "pale gold", "yellow", "black"), ])
pal$family <- c(rep("Red", 3), rep("Blue", 3), rep("Green", 3), rep("Orange", 3), rep("Gold", 3), "Yellow", "Black")
pal$step <- c(1:3, 1:3, 1:3, 1:3, 1:3, 1, 1)
pal$family <- factor(pal$family, levels = rev(unique(pal$family)))
pal$label <- paste0(pal$ink, "\n", pal$hex, ifelse(is.na(pal$charts), "", paste0("\n", pal$charts, " charts")))
ggplot(pal, aes(step, family)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = hex), width = 0.92, height = 0.85) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label, colour = ifelse(farver::decode_colour(hex, to = "hcl")[, "l"] > 60, "#000000", "#ffffff")),
    size = 2.7, lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = c("Dark", "Mid", "Light"), position = "top") +
  labs(
    title = "House Colors",
    subtitle = "Colors measured on the charts, Oct. 2011 to July 2014",
    caption = paste0("Source: ", format(n_all, big.mark = ","), " WSJ web graphics")
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

```{r palette-periods, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  inks[, c("ink", "hex", "A", "B", "C", "D", "Asia", "US", "charts")],
  col.names = c("Color", "Hex", "A", "B", "C", "D", "Asia", "U.S.", "All"),
  caption = "Charts using each measured color, by period and by desk, of all charts."
)
```

The two groups of desks used the same swatches, to the hex value, but not equally. The Asia desks lean on the mid shades, red, steel blue, and green; the U.S. desks on red and the dark shades, navy and dark green, measured on `r inks$US[inks$ink == "navy"]` and `r inks$US[inks$ink == "dark green"]` U.S. charts against `r inks$US[inks$ink == "steel"]` for steel blue. Navy and dark green: `r cite(c("MK-BT730_MSOFT_NS_20120419183018.jpg", "MK-BV957_UPS_NS_20120724173912.jpg", "MK-BX952_PITTMA_NS_20121014184805.jpg"))`.
A stronger blue, `#0074a5`, on `r inks$charts[inks$ink == "blue"]` charts, is not in the palettes.
`wsj_pal()` holds the colors in the palettes described below; `ggthemes_data$wsj$palettes` has the hex values.

Orange is the one hue the charts used in only two shades. Its third, `#fdd1ab`, is not measured: it is a 55% tint of the mid orange, the tint that makes the light shade of every other family (see the next section).

### Period A's bright set

Before the redesign of October 2011 the U.S. desks drew with a set of saturated colors on white: royal blue `r wsj_col("royal blue")`, red `r wsj_col("bright red")`, green `r wsj_col("bright green")`, black and a pure yellow `r wsj_col("bright yellow")`, with pale shades of the first three, `r wsj_col("pale royal blue")`, `r wsj_col("pale bright red")` and `r wsj_col("pale bright green")`. The royal blue is on `r inks$US[inks$ink == "royal blue"]` U.S. charts of the period and the red on `r inks$US[inks$ink == "bright red"]`; none of the set appears after September 2011. Royal blue usually leads: a single series is red or royal blue, and charts of two or more series mostly start with the blue. Red and blue: `r cite(c("MK-BL067_SOUTHW_NS_20110404181215.jpg", "P1-BB372A_TRADE_NS_20110628174503.jpg"))`; royal blue alone: `r cite("NA-BK096_SHORTA_NS_20110131183003.jpg")`; four colors: `r cite("NA-BK291_SPENDo_NS_20110214123602.jpg")`. The Asia charts of the period use the red and the green, and only one the royal blue. `wsj_pal("bright")` and `wsj_pal("bright_light")` hold the set.

```{r bright, fig.width = 3.4, fig.height = 4.2}
## After "Three Partners": imports and exports by country, on white, with a sans title.
trade <- data.frame(
  country = factor(rep(c("S. Korea", "Colombia", "Panama"), 2), levels = c("S. Korea", "Colombia", "Panama")),
  flow = factor(rep(c("Imports", "Exports"), each = 3), levels = c("Imports", "Exports")),
  value = c(48, 16, 0.4, 37, 11, 5.8)
)
ggplot(trade, aes(country, value, fill = flow)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Imports = wsj_pal("bright")(2)[2], Exports = wsj_pal("bright")(1)), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(prefix = "$", suffix = " billion"), breaks = seq(0, 50, 10),
                     limits = c(0, 50), expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(title = "Three Partners", subtitle = "U.S. trade by country, 2010",
       caption = "Source: U.S. International Trade Commission") +
  on_field("white") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(family = wsj_text_semibold, face = "plain"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(family = wsj_text_semibold, face = subtitle_face_ab),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left", axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

The data are approximate readings of `r cite("P1-BB372A_TRADE_NS_20110628174503.jpg")`.

### How the shades were built

The shades are tints: each lighter color is a darker one mixed toward white in RGB, as a tint slider in Illustrator or an opacity over white makes it. They are not steps of HSL lightness or HSB brightness, and they are not web-safe values. The fit of each relation is the share of the base color, `t` in 255 - t (255 - base), and the worst of the three channels' misses, in levels of 255:

```{r tints, echo = FALSE}
tints <- data.frame(
  shade = c("pale red", "pale steel", "pale green", "pale gold", "salmon", "tan", "light orange", "steel", "green",
            "ivory field", "ivory band", "gray field", "gray band", "pale blue field", "pale green field"),
  color = c("#ebb3a4", "#abbdcb", "#afccae", "#e8dbaf", "#d5695d", "#d3ba68", "#fcac67", "#5d8ca8", "#65a479",
            "#f8f2e4", "#efe4c9", "#efefef", "#dddddd", "#eff4f9", "#f2f9f2"),
  of = c("salmon", "steel", "green", "tan", "red", "gold", "orange", "navy", "dark green", "gold", "gold", "black",
         "black", "steel", "green"),
  base = c("#d5695d", "#5d8ca8", "#65a479", "#d3ba68", "#c72e29", "#be9c2e", "#fb832d", "#016392", "#098154",
           "#be9c2e", "#be9c2e", "#000000", "#000000", "#5d8ca8", "#65a479")
)
fit <- t(mapply(tint_of, tints$base, tints$color))
tints$tint <- paste0(round(100 * fit[, "t"]), "%")
tints$miss <- round(fit[, "miss"], 1)
knitr::kable(tints[, c("shade", "color", "of", "base", "tint", "miss")],
             col.names = c("Shade", "Color", "Tint of", "Base", "Share of base", "Worst miss"), row.names = FALSE)
```

- Every light shade is a 53 to 56% tint of the mid shade of its family, to within a few levels: most likely a 55% tint, a round value a designer would set, which fits all four as well as their own best values do and much better than 50 or 60%. The mid red, gold, and orange are 71 to 74% tints of their dark shades.
- Navy and dark green are not tints: they miss by 13 and 17 levels, and dark green is a bluer hue than the green. They are swatches of their own, darker and more saturated, which is how the charts use them, for highlighted bars.
- The fields and bands are tints too: the ivory field is a 13% tint of the gold and its bands 26%; the gray field is 6% black and its bands 13%; the pale blue and green fields are 9% tints of the steel and the green. The band is about twice the field.
- The pale blue field, its bands, the pale steel, the steel, and the navy make a five-step ramp of measured colors, light to dark: `scale_fill_gradient_wsj()` and `scale_colour_gradient_wsj()` use it by default, as `"steel"`. The charts' grays are neutral tints of black too, so the pale partner of black in `wsj_pal("categorical_light")` is `#bdbdbd`, about 26% black.

So the desk worked from a few base swatches and made the rest as RGB tints. That suits web graphics, and explains why the colors do not fall on round CMYK values under a press profile: they were never ink specifications.

### On each field

Most of the charts that use the palettes are on ivory, but the palettes appear on every field. The swatches of each `wsj_pal()` palette, then the same chart, on the five fields of the corpus, each a `paper` of `theme_wsj()`: ivory and gray, the pale blue `#eff4f9` and white of period A, and the pale green `#f2f9f2` of the PMI charts. The pale tints lose most against gray and pale blue; keep them for fills.

```{r palettes-fields, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.8}
palettes <- c("categorical", "categorical_light", "categorical_dark", "direction", "comparison", "actual_forecast",
              "blues", "greens", "reds", "golds", "oranges")
sw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(palettes, function(p) {
  cols <- wsj_pal(p)(attr(wsj_pal(p), "max_n"))
  data.frame(palette = p, i = seq_along(cols), hex = cols)
}))
sw$palette <- factor(sw$palette, levels = rev(palettes))
swatches <- function(paper) {
  ggplot(sw, aes(i, palette, fill = hex)) +
    geom_tile(width = 0.85, height = 0.7) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
    labs(title = field_name(paper), subtitle = fields[[paper]]) +
    on_field(paper, base_size = 9) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.9)))
}
side_by_side(lapply(names(fields), swatches))
```

```{r palettes-fields-chart, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.8}
## Stacked columns in the three greens, the darkest at the base.
stack <- expand.grid(year = 2008:2013, part = c("Completed", "Under way", "Planned"))
stack$part <- factor(stack$part, levels = c("Planned", "Under way", "Completed"))
stack$value <- c(3.4, 3.9, 4.4, 5.6, 6.5, 7.6, 1.0, 1.6, 2.2, 2.4, 2.9, 3.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.4, 1.5, 2.0, 2.6)
chart <- function(paper) {
  ggplot(stack, aes(year, value)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = part), width = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(wsj_pal("greens")(3), c("Completed", "Under way", "Planned"))) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2008, 2010, 2012), labels = c("2008", "'10", "'12")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 14, 4), limits = c(0, 14), expand = expansion(0)) +
    labs(title = field_name(paper), fill = NULL) +
    on_field(paper, base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.75)), legend.key.size = unit(8, "pt"))
}
side_by_side(lapply(names(fields), chart))
```

### One series, two series, more

- **One series is red, or a blue or green.** Of the charts read with one data series, from the redesign on, `r by_desk(single, series_colors == "red", TRUE, "single-series charts")` draw it in red. The second choice differs: steel blue on the Asia desks (`r pct(single$series_colors == "steel_blue" & single$desks == "Asia", single$desks == "Asia")`), navy or dark green on the U.S. desks (`r pct(single$series_colors %in% c("dark_blue", "dark_green") & single$desks == "US", single$desks == "US")`, against `r pct(single$series_colors == "steel_blue" & single$desks == "US", single$desks == "US")` for steel blue). Red: `r cite(c("AI-BU349_SPAIN_NS_20120719113903.jpg", "AM-AU378_CHINAH_NS_20120820083604.jpg"))`; steel blue: `r cite("AI-BN971_JECON_NS_20111010233303.jpg")`; navy and dark green: `r cite(c("MK-BT730_MSOFT_NS_20120419183018.jpg", "MK-BV957_UPS_NS_20120724173912.jpg"))`.
- **Two series are red and a blue or green.** On the Asia desks red and steel blue is the most common pair: `r cite(c("AI-BU867_Econom_NS_20120809135703.jpg", "AI-BO486_CPROPc_NS_20111102132703.jpg"))`. The U.S. desks pair red with dark green, navy, or steel blue about equally often: `r cite(c("MK-BW709_LIQUOR_NS_20120823175703.jpg", "NA-BO063_CAPJOU_NS_20111107182113.jpg"))`. Both also pair two shades of one hue, dark and pale.
- **Three or more lines take distinct hues.** Charts rarely show more than five lines.

  On the Asia desks the lines are red, steel blue, and green, then black and gold. Of the `r sum(many_lines$desks == "Asia")` Asia line charts with three or more series, `r sum(has_colour(many_lines[many_lines$desks == "Asia", ], "black"))` add black and `r sum(has_colour(many_lines[many_lines$desks == "Asia", ], "gold"))` gold. `wsj_pal()` takes them in that order, though so few charts cannot settle it: `r cite(c("AI-CC875_ARATES_NS_20130814225706.jpg", "AM-BC480_INDIAH_NS_20140227104505.jpg", "AI-BZ169_CINTER_NS_20130219061204.jpg"))`. 

  The U.S. desks use their darker trio, red, navy, and dark green, then black and orange more often than gold. Of `r sum(many_lines$desks == "US")` such charts read, `r sum(has_colour(many_lines[many_lines$desks == "US", ], "black"))` add black, `r sum(grepl("orange", many_lines$series_colors[many_lines$desks == "US"]))` orange and `r sum(has_colour(many_lines[many_lines$desks == "US", ], "gold"))` gold. `wsj_pal("categorical_us")` puts black before orange, though the two are about equally common: `r cite(c("MK-BQ175_Yahoo_NS_20111102182103.jpg", "P1-BC783_SPRINT_NS_20111003200612.jpg", "MK-CK818_GREENB_NS_20140316183603.jpg"))`.

  On both, a gray line is a benchmark set behind the others: `r cite(c("AI-CA003_CRT_NS_20130329012403.jpg", "AI-CH135_JDEFLA_NS_20140306045703.jpg"))`.
- **Three or more bars, segments, or slices take families of hues.** Categories that belong together share a hue in its dark, mid, and pale shades, and the next group takes the next hue. Of the `r nrow(many_parts)` bar and pie charts with three or more series, `r sum(many_parts$shades)` print two or more shades of one hue, measured: `r cite(c("AI-CC605_JSMART_NS_20130731070306.jpg", "AI-CC842A_APURS_NS_20130813000004.jpg", "AM-BB223_AMONEY_NS_20131126013004.jpg", "AM-BB786_GLPHER_NS_20140108021203.jpg"))`. Use the `"blues"`, `"greens"`, `"reds"`, `"golds"` and `"oranges"` palettes, a family to each group.

Lines are about 2 pixels wide on a 225-pixel graphic, a medium weight (`r share(asia$line_weight == "medium", sum(asia$line_weight != ""), "Asia line charts")`): `r cite(c("AI-BU349_SPAIN_NS_20120719113903.jpg", "AI-BR349_JECON_NS_20120311232103.jpg"))`. `linewidth = 0.8` matches at the sizes used here. The U.S. charts are often larger, and the reading of their line weight is not comparable.

```{r two-series}
set.seed(5)
d <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("2011-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 30), series = "Imports",
             value = 240 - 0.9 * 1:30 + stats::rnorm(30, 0, 3)),
  data.frame(date = seq(as.Date("2011-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 30), series = "Exports",
             value = 150 + 1.3 * 1:30 + stats::rnorm(30, 0, 3))
)
## Imports first, so they take the palette's red.
d$series <- factor(d$series, levels = c("Imports", "Exports"))
ends <- d[d$date == max(d$date), ]
ggplot(d, aes(date, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_label(
    data = ends, aes(label = series, fill = series), colour = "#ffffff", fontface = "bold", size = 3,
    hjust = 1, vjust = -0.4, label.r = unit(0, "pt"), label.size = 0
  ) +
  scale_colour_wsj() +
  scale_fill_wsj() +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(paste0(2011:2013, "-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(prefix = "$", suffix = " billion"), breaks = seq(125, 275, 25)) +
  guides(colour = "none", fill = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Narrowing",
    subtitle = "The trade deficit shrank as\nexports rose and imports fell.",
    caption = "Note: Data are seasonally adjusted\nSource: Commerce Department\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

The labels above copy the tinted label boxes of `r cite("AI-BU867_Econom_NS_20120809135703.jpg")`.

```{r families}
## After "Seeking Cash": a hue to each group, and the pale shade for the year to date.
cash <- expand.grid(year = 2009:2013, group = c("Developers", "Fund managers"))
cash$value <- c(0.7, 0.4, 2.6, 2.2, 3.4, 0.6, 1.6, 2.8, 1.6, 3.9)
cash$shade <- paste(cash$group, ifelse(cash$year == 2013, "to date", "full year"))
## The groups sit side by side on one axis, a gap between them.
cash$x <- cash$year - 2008 + ifelse(cash$group == "Fund managers", 6, 0)
shades <- c(
  `Developers full year` = wsj_pal("greens")(3)[2], `Developers to date` = wsj_pal("greens")(3)[3],
  `Fund managers full year` = wsj_pal("blues")(3)[2], `Fund managers to date` = wsj_pal("blues")(3)[3]
)
ggplot(cash, aes(x, value, fill = shade)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = c(3, 9), y = 4.4, label = c("Developers", "Fund managers"), size = 3,
           family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = shades, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cash$x[cash$year %% 2 == 1],
                     labels = c("2009", "'11", "'13\nYTD")[(cash$year[cash$year %% 2 == 1] - 2007) / 2]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(prefix = "$", suffix = " billion"), breaks = 0:4, limits = c(0, 4.6),
                     expand = expansion(0)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seeking Cash",
    subtitle = "Capital raised for real-estate funds,\nin U.S. dollars",
    caption = wsj_caption("PERE")
  ) +
  theme_wsj(paper = "gray", base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

The data are made up; the form follows `r cite("AM-BB223_AMONEY_NS_20131126013004.jpg")`, which runs each group in green or steel blue and gives the year to date the pale shade.

### Gains and losses

Charts of change color gains green and losses red. The colors are common on the Asia desks and rarer on the U.S. desks. Of all the charts read, `r by_desk(read, direction_colors == "True")` use them. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-BW723_JECON_NS_20121030003018.jpg", "AI-BY972_JECON_NS_20130207023903.jpg", "AI-BT650_JECON_NS_20120620002102.jpg"))`.
The commonest pair is green `#65a479` with red `#c72e29`, `wsj_pal("direction")`; some charts use the darker green `#098154` or the softer red `#d5695d` instead, as in `r cite("MK-CI701_FORD_NS_20131218184503.jpg")`.

### Elections

The U.S. desks' election charts of 2011 to 2013 use the house colors, not party colors of their own: the Democratic candidate in navy or steel blue and the Republican in red `#c72e29`, with the pale shades for subgroups. Examples: `r cite(c("NA-BO063_CAPJOU_NS_20111107182113.jpg", "NA-BT048_WOMENV_NS_20121017183908.jpg"))`. `wsj_pal("party")` keeps the colors of the old `"dem_rep"` palette and is not measured; to match these charts, use `c(wsj_pal("comparison")(1), wsj_pal()(1))`.

A poll by group sets the two candidates back to back from a common middle, the Democrat on the left. Each value is printed in white at the outer end of its bar, with the unit only on the first row.

```{r election, fig.width = 4.4, fig.height = 3.4}
## After "Generation Gap": the Democrat in navy, the Republican in red.
ages <- c("18–34", "35–49", "50–64", "65 and older")
poll <- data.frame(
  age = factor(rep(ages, 2), levels = rev(ages)),
  candidate = rep(c("Obama", "Romney"), each = 4),
  share = c(54, 46, 54, 38, 37, 45, 41, 54)
)
poll$x <- ifelse(poll$candidate == "Obama", -poll$share, poll$share)
poll$label <- ifelse(poll$age == ages[1], paste0(poll$share, "%"), poll$share)
party_cols <- c(Obama = wsj_pal("comparison")(1), Romney = wsj_pal()(1))
ggplot(poll, aes(x, age)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = candidate), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = x - sign(x) * 1.5, label = label, hjust = ifelse(x < 0, 0, 1)), colour = "#ffffff", size = 3,
            family = wsj_text_semibold) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-2, 2), y = 4.65, label = c("OBAMA", "ROMNEY"), colour = party_cols,
           hjust = c(1, 0), size = 3, family = wsj_text_semibold) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = party_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-60, 60), breaks = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Generation Gap", subtitle = "Support in a match-up for president, by age",
       caption = wsj_caption("WSJ/NBC News poll, Nov. 2–5, 2011")) +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

The data are approximate readings of `r cite("NA-BO063_CAPJOU_NS_20111107182113.jpg")`.

### Above and below a threshold

Indexes with a natural middle, such as a purchasing managers' index (50 divides expansion from contraction) or a sentiment index (0), fill the area between the line and that middle: green above, red below. A black line runs on top, and an arrow bar beside the panel names the two directions, "Expanding" and "Contracting", or "Positive" and "Negative" with the index's name between them. About two dozen Asia charts are drawn this way, nearly all of them the HSBC China PMI from 2011 to 2013; the fills are the mid green `#65a479` and the salmon `#d5695d` from 2012, bright green and red before. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-BV139_CECON_NS_20120823021803.jpg", "AI-BV546_JECON_NS_20120911064506.jpg", "AI-BQ917_CECON_NS_20120221233902.jpg", "AI-BN572_CHINAP_NS_20110922002103.jpg"))`.
Draw the fill with `geom_wsj_threshold()` and the arrows with `wsj_direction_bar()`; both need room outside the panel.

```{r threshold, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4}
pmi <- data.frame(
  month = seq(as.Date("2011-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 20),
  index = c(54.5, 51.7, 51.8, 51.8, 51.6, 50.1, 49.3, 49.9, 49.9, 51, 47.7, 48.7, 48.8, 49.6, 48.3, 48.7, 48.4, 49.3,
            48.5, 47.8)
)
p1 <- ggplot(pmi, aes(month, index)) +
  geom_wsj_threshold(threshold = 50) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50) +
  geom_line() +
  ## The latest value: a ringed point and plain bold text.
  annotate("point", x = max(pmi$month), y = 47.8, shape = 21, size = 2.5, fill = fields[["ivory"]], stroke = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = max(pmi$month), y = 46.9, label = "August: 47.8*", hjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 3,
           family = wsj_text_font) +
  ## On the left the bar has to clear the y labels.
  wsj_direction_bar(50, side = "left", offset = 24, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2011-01-01", "2012-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(46, 54, 2), limits = c(46, 55)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "HSBC\u2019s China PMI",
    caption = "Source: Markit Economics     *Preliminary\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0), plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 34))
sentiment <- data.frame(
  quarter = seq(as.Date("2010-01-01"), by = "quarter", length.out = 12),
  index = c(-2, 4, 7, -5, -1, -22, 7, -2, -2.5, -3, -2.8, 2.2)
)
p2 <- ggplot(sentiment, aes(quarter, index)) +
  geom_wsj_threshold() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_line() +
  wsj_callout(max(sentiment$quarter), 2.2, "3Q: 2.2", nudge_x = -18, nudge_y = 22, family = wsj_text_font) +
  wsj_direction_bar(0, labels = c("Positive", "Negative"), title = "SENTIMENT", offset = 10, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(paste0(2010:2012, "-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-30, 20, 10), limits = c(-30, 20)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Feeling Better", subtitle = "Index of large Japanese\ncompanies\u2019 sentiment",
       caption = "Source: Ministry of Finance\nThe Wall Street Journal") +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0), plot.margin = margin(10, 30, 10, 10))
side_by_side(list(p1, p2))
```

The data are approximate readings of the two charts cited first.

### Highlighting

To pick out one bar, WSJ charts darken it within its own hue and set its label in bold. They do not gray out the rest.
A steel-blue ranking highlights in navy, a green one in dark green, a salmon one in red: `r cite(c("AI-CD614_VIETWE_NS_20130918063008.jpg", "AI-BU730_PHILBA_NS_20120806050005.jpg", "AM-BD893_CDEBT_NS_20140616115704.jpg", "AI-CF229_BANGWA_NS_20131203125403.jpg"))`.
`wsj_pal("comparison")` gives the blue pair; the `"greens"`, `"reds"` and `"golds"` palettes give the others, darkest first.

Ranked horizontal bars drop the value axis: the category is labeled on the left, the value at the end of each bar, and rows are separated by dotted rules or bands.

```{r highlight, fig.height = 4.4, warning = FALSE}
d <- data.frame(
  country = c("Colombia", "Vietnam", "Turkey", "Ukraine", "Egypt", "China", "Chile", "India", "Thailand"),
  growth = c(278, 266, 247, 237, 211, 209, 209, 189, 176)
)
d$country <- factor(d$country, levels = rev(d$country))
d$focal <- d$country == "Vietnam"
ggplot(d, aes(growth, country)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = focal), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(growth, ifelse(country == "Colombia", "%", "")),
                fontface = ifelse(focal, "bold", "plain")),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = wsj_pal("comparison")(2)[1], `FALSE` = wsj_pal("comparison")(2)[2]),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Going Mobile",
    subtitle = "Growth in active smart devices,\nJanuary 2012 to January 2013",
    caption = wsj_caption("Flurry Analytics")
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#8a8a8a", linewidth = 0.25, linetype = "dotted"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = ifelse(levels(d$country) == "Vietnam", "bold", "plain"))
  )
```

### Shades of one hue

Stacked bars and pies fill their segments with the shades of one or two hues, labeled at the side with short leader lines rather than a legend: `r cite(c("AI-CC842A_APURS_NS_20130813000004.jpg", "AI-CC605_JSMART_NS_20130731070306.jpg", "AI-BU352_SINGBE_NS_20120720041503.jpg"))`.
Forecasts and estimates take the pale shade of the actual values' hue: `r cite(c("AI-BQ213_SINGHc_NS_20120119073303.jpg", "AI-CE420_AVOTE_NS_20131024043004.jpg", "AI-BS155_SKECON_NS_20120416015702.jpg"))`. `wsj_pal("actual_forecast")` is the steel-blue pair, and `wsj_pal("categorical_light")` has the pale shade of every hue.

```{r forecast}
d <- data.frame(year = 2004:2014, value = c(4.3, 5.8, 3.9, 8.5, 7.5, 9.6, 9.7, 9.3, 6.9, 7.9, 6.8))
d$kind <- ifelse(d$year >= 2013, "forecast", "actual")
ggplot(d, aes(year, value, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 13.5 + 2000, y = 8.6, label = "Forecast*", hjust = 0.5, size = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(actual = wsj_col("orange"), forecast = wsj_col("light orange")), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2004, 2014, 2), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Sputtering Engine",
    subtitle = "GDP growth rate",
    caption = "*Forecast from finance ministry\nSource: Government statistics\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font)
```

## Labels and callouts

- **Direct labels first.** Series are named beside the data, in the series' own color, on `r by_desk(read, has(labelling, "direct_series_labels"), lengths(strsplit(series_colors, ";")) >= 2, "charts with two or more series")`: `r cite(c("AI-BG392_QE2REA_NS_20101104140201.jpg", "MK-BW709_LIQUOR_NS_20120823175703.jpg", "MK-BU489A_AMC_NS_20120521183610.jpg"))`. A legend at the top appears on `r sum(has(read$labelling, "legend_top"))` charts read, usually where lines cross too often to label or bars are grouped: `r cite(c("AI-BU867_Econom_NS_20120809135703.jpg", "AI-CC875_ARATES_NS_20130814225706.jpg", "P1-BB372A_TRADE_NS_20110628174503.jpg"))`.
- **Labels take the line's own color**, usually in bold, not a lighter or darker shade of it. Measured on `r nrow(label_colors)` label and line pairs in `r length(unique(label_colors$file))` charts, `r by_desk(label_colors, abs(dL) <= 4, TRUE, "pairs")` match within 4 units of lightness (L\*). On the Asia charts most of the rest are artifacts of the measurement: a pale fill or band taken for the line makes the label read darker than its line, and once a dark highlighted bar taken for the line makes it read lighter, `r cite("AI-CI160_AUSTOU_NS_20140424054805.jpg")`. A black series gets a black label. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-BG392_QE2REA_NS_20101104140201.jpg", "AI-BV752_CPANET_NS_20120919115707.jpg", "AM-BA985_CMATTE_NS_20131107123008.jpg"))`. Map the label's color to the same variable as the line's, as in `geom_text(aes(colour = series))`, and the scale gives both the same color.
- **Callouts mark the latest value.** A number callout holds the value, often after its date ("July 4.6%", "2Q: 0.7%"), in bold type inside a filled box or circle, with a triangular tail pointing at the bar or the end of the line. Draw them with `wsj_callout()`.

  Of the `r nrow(callouts)` charts with one, `r share(callouts$tail == "triangle", nrow(callouts), "callouts")` have the tail and `r share(callouts$marks_latest == "True", nrow(callouts), "callouts")` mark the latest value.

  Callouts are black with white type (`r sum(callouts$fill == "black")`) or yellow `#ffe03d` with black type (`r sum(callouts$fill == "yellow")`). The other `r sum(!callouts$fill %in% c("black", "yellow"))` take a color of the chart: the color of the series they mark, with white type, as in `r cite(c("AI-BR167_CGDP_NS_20120304224503.jpg", "AI-CF617A_ASIAS_NS_20131223122404.jpg", "NA-BQ947_STUDEN_NS_20120531123606.jpg", "MK-CJ995_TWITTE_NS_20140210182103.jpg"))`, or on the Asia desks another shade, mostly the mid steel blue `#5d8ca8` with white type, as in `r cite(c("AI-CF534_BITCOI_NS_20131218055104.jpg", "AI-BW283_SKRATE_NS_20121010224803.jpg"))`, and once the pale shades with black type, `r cite("AI-BY764_IECON_NS_20130129031805.jpg")`. A chart with two marked series gives each callout its series' color. Black: `r cite(c("AI-BV492_JECON_NS_20120909223903.jpg", "AI-BS026_JECON_NS_20120410232103.jpg"))`. Yellow: `r cite(c("AI-BV612_SKRATE_NS_20120913002402.jpg", "AI-BV557_JECON_NS_20120911225702.jpg", "MK-BT552_EBOOKS_NS_20120412173602.jpg"))`.

  Most are boxes; the U.S. desks also drew large black circles with a tail, `r cite(c("MK-BW709_LIQUOR_NS_20120823175703.jpg", "MK-BV957_UPS_NS_20120724173912.jpg"))`. Most sit above the point, often to its left (`r share(grepl("above", callouts$position), nrow(callouts), "callouts")`), and below it when the value is low.

  On the Asia desks callouts belong to periods B and C: only `r sum(callouts$period == "D" & callouts$desks == "Asia")` of the `r sum(asia$period == "D")` Asia charts of period D have one, and the rest mark the latest value with a pointer label (see [below](#pointers-rings-arrows-and-markers)) or plain text, if at all. The U.S. desks kept them, on `r share(callouts$period == "D" & callouts$desks == "US", us_read$period == "D", "U.S. charts read")` of period D: `r cite(c("MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg", "MK-CI701_FORD_NS_20131218184503.jpg"))`.

```{r callout, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.8}
## The callouts of the three cited charts: a black box on a bar, a yellow circle on the end of a step line, and a
## yellow box on the end of a line. Offsets are in points; clip = "off" lets a callout cross the panel edge.
thm <- theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font)
gdp <- data.frame(quarter = 1:6, change = c(-7.9, -1.3, 6.8, 0.3, 5.2, 0.7))
gdp$sign <- factor(ifelse(gdp$change >= 0, "positive", "negative"), levels = c("positive", "negative"))
p1 <- ggplot(gdp, aes(quarter, change, fill = sign)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.95) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  wsj_callout(6, 0.7, "2Q:\n0.7%", shape = "rounded", nudge_x = -4, nudge_y = 34, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_fill_wsj("direction", guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = c("1Q\n2011", "2Q", "3Q", "4Q", "1Q\n'12", "2Q")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(-8, 8, 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Japan\u2019s GDP", subtitle = "Annualized change from prior\nquarter, seasonally adjusted") +
  thm +
  theme(axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
rate <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(c("2009-01-01", "2010-07-01", "2010-11-01", "2011-01-01", "2011-03-01", "2011-06-01", "2012-07-01",
                   "2012-10-01")),
  value = c(2, 2.25, 2.5, 2.75, 3, 3.25, 3, 3)
)
p2 <- ggplot(rate, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_step(colour = wsj_pal("blues")(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  wsj_callout(as.Date("2012-10-01"), 3, "3.0%", fill = "yellow", shape = "circle", nudge_x = -16, nudge_y = -26,
              family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(paste0(2009:2012, "-01-01")), labels = c("2009", "2010", "2011", "2012")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = 0:5, limits = c(0, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Keeping Steady", subtitle = "Bank of Korea key policy rate") +
  thm +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
orders <- data.frame(month = 1:7, change = c(0.6, 2.5, -2.8, 5.5, -14.8, 5.6, 4.6))
p3 <- ggplot(orders, aes(month, change)) +
  geom_line(colour = wsj_pal("blues")(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  wsj_callout(7, 4.6, "July 4.6%", fill = "yellow", nudge_x = -10, nudge_y = 26, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7, labels = c("J", "F", "M", "A", "M", "J", "J")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(-15, 5, 5)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Better Than Expected", subtitle = "Core machinery orders,\nchange from previous month") +
  thm
side_by_side(list(p1, p2, p3))
```

```{r callout-series, fig.width = 3.2, fig.height = 4.2}
## After "China's GDP": each callout in the color of the series it marks, and the label text inside it.
gdp <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2005:2012, 2),
  series = rep(c("Actual", "Target"), each = 8),
  rate = c(11.3, 12.7, 14.2, 9.6, 9.2, 10.4, 9.2, NA, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 7.5)
)
gdp$series <- factor(gdp$series, levels = c("Actual", "Target"))
cols <- c(Actual = wsj_col("red"), Target = wsj_col("navy"))
ggplot(gdp[!is.na(gdp$rate), ], aes(year, rate, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  wsj_callout(2011, 9.2, "Actual\n9.2%", fill = cols[["Actual"]], nudge_x = -6, nudge_y = 26, size = 3.4,
              family = wsj_text_font) +
  wsj_callout(2012, 7.5, "Target\n7.5%", fill = cols[["Target"]], nudge_x = -14, nudge_y = -24, size = 3.4,
              family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2005:2012, labels = c("2005", paste0("'0", 6:9), "'10", "'11", "'12")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(0, 14, 2), limits = c(0, 14.5)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "China\u2019s GDP",
    subtitle = "Annual targeted and actual\ngrowth rate",
    caption = "Sources: National Bureau of Statistics;\nWen Jiabao\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font)
```

### Pointers, rings, arrows, and markers

Four more marks are rarer than the callouts, but recur. The lists of examples below were drawn up from the Asia charts.

- **Pointer labels.** After the gray field arrives, the boxed callout gives way to plain type: the date in regular weight and the value in bold, "3Q: **+3.5%**", with a small black wedge pointing at the point or bar. All `r length(annotated$pointer)` Asia charts found with one are from period D: `r cite(annotated$pointer[c(5, 8, 4, 2)])`.
- **Rings.** The latest point of a line can be ringed: an open black circle, filled with the field, usually beside a pointer label or plain text (`r length(annotated$ring)` charts): `r cite(annotated$ring[c(2, 5, 6)])`. Draw it with `geom_point(shape = 21)`. In late 2011 and early 2012 a few red lines carried a dot on every observation instead: `r cite(c("AI-BP106_JECON_NS_20111130010303.jpg", "AI-BP835_CPROP_NS_20120104011203.jpg"))`.
- **Direction arrows.** A currency chart says which way is which with a broad pale arrow beside the line, labeled with what the direction means, "Weaker yuan" or "Stronger yen" (`r length(annotated$arrow)` charts): `r cite(annotated$arrow)`. An inverted scale is flagged in a note instead (see [Axes](#axes)).
- **Event markers.** A thin gray vertical rule marks the moment of an event, labeled beside it, or a shaded span marks the time after it (`r length(annotated$event)` charts): `r cite(annotated$event)`.

```{r annotations, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.2}
## After "Target the Line", "A New Day" and "Shifting Currency", with made-up data.
thm <- theme_wsj(base_size = 10, paper = "gray", base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
set.seed(6)
cpi <- walk(26, 9.8, 0.35, from = "2012-01-01")
cpi$value[26] <- 9.9
last <- cpi[26, ]
p1 <- ggplot(cpi, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = wsj_col("dark green"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  ## The ring, then the pointer label below it.
  geom_point(data = last, shape = 21, size = 2.6, stroke = 0.6, fill = fields[["gray"]]) +
  wedge(last$date - 12, last$value - 0.35, "up", w = 22, h = 0.35) +
  annotate("text", x = last$date - 4, y = last$value - 1.1, label = 'plain("December: ")*bold("9.9%")',
           parse = TRUE, hjust = 1, size = 3, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(c("2012-01-01", "2013-01-01", "2014-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%", accuracy = 0.1), breaks = seq(5, 12.5, 2.5),
                     limits = c(5, 12.5), expand = expansion(0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Target the Line", subtitle = "Consumer prices,\nyear-on-year change",
       caption = wsj_caption("Government of India")) +
  thm
prices <- data.frame(year = 2009:2014, change = c(28, 20, 11, 26, 8, -0.5))
p2 <- ggplot(prices, aes(year, change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = change >= 0), width = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  ## The pointer sits left of the small bar, below the zero line, its wedge on the bar's corner.
  wedge(2013.6, -1.1, "right", w = 0.18, h = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2013.4, y = -1.3, label = 'bold("-0.5%")', parse = TRUE, hjust = 1, size = 3,
           family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = wsj_col("green"), `FALSE` = wsj_col("red")), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2009:2014, labels = c("2009", "'10", "'11", "'12", "'13", "'14*")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%"), breaks = seq(-5, 30, 5), limits = c(-5, 30)) +
  labs(title = "A New Day", subtitle = "Change in average\nhouse prices",
       caption = "*First two months\nSource: Hong Kong government\nThe Wall Street Journal") +
  thm +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
set.seed(7)
yuan <- walk(40, 6.6, 0.012, -0.007, from = "2010-06-01")
p3 <- ggplot(yuan, aes(date, value)) +
  ## The event: a gray rule, labeled beside it with a wedge.
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2010-06-19"), colour = "#a6a6a6", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2010-08-20"), y = 6.73, label = "Peg ends", hjust = 0, size = 2.8,
           family = wsj_text_font) +
  wedge(as.Date("2010-06-25"), 6.73, "left", w = 45, h = 0.02) +
  geom_line(colour = wsj_col("red"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  ## The direction arrow, pale, above the line with its label below: up is a weaker yuan. The head is centered on
  ## the shaft.
  annotate("polygon", x = as.Date("2013-04-01") + c(-25, -25, -55, 0, 55, 25, 25),
           y = c(6.66, 6.72, 6.72, 6.78, 6.72, 6.72, 6.66), fill = "#bdbdbd") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2013-04-01"), y = 6.645, label = "Weaker\nyuan", size = 2.8, lineheight = 0.9,
           vjust = 1, family = wsj_text_font) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(paste0(2011:2013, "-01-01")), labels = wsj_year_label()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(6.0, 6.8, 0.2), limits = c(5.95, 6.8), labels = scales::label_number(0.1)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Shifting Currency", subtitle = "How many yuan one U.S. dollar buys",
       caption = wsj_caption("WSJ Market Data Group")) +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))
side_by_side(list(p1, p2, p3))
```

## Chart types

```{r types, echo = FALSE}
count_types <- function(d) table(factor(unlist(strsplit(d$chart_types, ";")), levels = names(types)))
types <- sort(table(unlist(strsplit(read$chart_types, ";"))), decreasing = TRUE)
types <- types[types >= 5]
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Type = gsub("_", " ", names(types)),
    Asia = paste0(round(100 * as.integer(count_types(asia)) / nrow(asia)), "%"),
    U.S. = paste0(round(100 * as.integer(count_types(us_read)) / nrow(us_read)), "%"),
    Charts = as.integer(types),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  caption = "Chart types of the charts read, as shares of each group of desks; a chart with two panels can count twice."
)
```

- **Columns** are as common as lines, and carry monthly and quarterly data as well as annual: `r cite(c("AI-BW723_JECON_NS_20121030003018.jpg", "MK-BT730_MSOFT_NS_20120419183018.jpg"))`. Gaps are narrow, less than a third of a bar on `r share(read$bar_gap == "narrow", sum(read$bar_gap != ""), "bar charts read")`: `geom_col(width = 0.8)` or more.
- **Lines** carry daily and monthly series: `r cite(c("AI-BR643_YUAN_NS_20120323043004.jpg", "MK-CH389_APPLE_NS_20131028180311.jpg"))`. On the Asia desks, steps carry policy rates (`r sum(has(asia$chart_types, "step"))` charts): `r cite("AI-BH794_BOK_NS_20110112225403.jpg")`.
- **Horizontal bars** are kept for rankings, sorted, with the values at the bar ends (see [Highlighting](#highlighting)): `r cite("MK-BX810_SODA_NS_20121008174503.jpg")`.
- **Pies** are rare (`r sum(has(read$chart_types, "pie") | has(read$chart_types, "donut"))` charts read, donuts included), with outside labels: `r cite("AI-BU352_SINGBE_NS_20120720041503.jpg")`.
- **Small multiples** are uncommon too: `r by_desk(read, as.integer(n_panels) > 1)` have more than one panel. A web graphic is one chart. See [Several panels](#several-panels).

### Several panels

When a chart has two or three panels, each is a chart of its own under the one title: a bold heading set flush left over the panel, often followed by the measure in regular weight, its own scale with its own unit on the top label, and often a different form, bars beside a line. The panels sit side by side with a wide gutter, or stacked. A threshold banner or a callout belongs to one panel, not to each. Examples: `r cite(c("AI-CB451_CECON_NS_20130609112404.jpg", "AI-CA484_AMONEY_NS_20130422223603.jpg", "AI-CC843_AMONEY_NS_20130813002103.jpg", "AI-BR132_ASIAEC_NS_20120301021803.jpg"))`.

`theme_wsj()` sets facet headings flush left and the panels two lines apart. Give each panel its own scale with `scales = "free_y"`, so `wsj_label()` marks the top label of each. Draw a different form in each panel by giving each layer its panel's rows, and put a callout or a banner in one panel by naming the panel: `wsj_callout(..., facets = list(panel = "Industrial production"))`.

```{r panels, fig.width = 6.4, fig.height = 4.2}
## After "Applying the Brakes": bars in one panel, a line in the other, each with its own scale and unit.
months <- seq(as.Date("2013-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = 5)
brakes <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = "Social financing, in trillions of yuan", month = months, value = c(2.5, 1.1, 2.5, 1.8, 1.2)),
  data.frame(panel = "Industrial production, change from a year earlier", month = months,
             value = c(9.9, 9.9, 8.9, 9.3, 9.2))
)
brakes$panel <- factor(brakes$panel, levels = unique(brakes$panel))
## A factor keeps the panels in order; a callout names its panel with a factor of the same levels.
panel <- function(i) factor(levels(brakes$panel)[i], levels = levels(brakes$panel))
first <- brakes[as.integer(brakes$panel) == 1, ]
second <- brakes[as.integer(brakes$panel) == 2, ]
ggplot(brakes, aes(month, value)) +
  geom_col(data = first, fill = wsj_col("steel"), width = 24) +
  geom_line(data = second, colour = wsj_col("green"), linewidth = 0.8) +
  wsj_callout(months[5], 1.2, "1.19", nudge_x = -2, nudge_y = 20, size = 2.8, family = wsj_text_font,
              facets = list(panel = panel(1))) +
  wsj_callout(months[5], 9.2, "9.2%", fill = "yellow", nudge_x = -6, nudge_y = 18, size = 2.8, family = wsj_text_font,
              facets = list(panel = panel(2))) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(24)) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = months, labels = c("J\n2013", "F", "M", "A", "M")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(), n.breaks = 4, expand = expansion(c(0, 0.1))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Applying the Brakes",
    subtitle = "China\u2019s regulators rein in financing, risking a slowdown in growth",
    caption = "Sources: People\u2019s Bank of China; National Bureau of Statistics\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(base_size = 10, base_family = wsj_text_font, title_family = wsj_title_font)
```

The data are made up; the second panel's axis does not start at zero, as a line's need not.

## With ggthemes

```{r recipe, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
ggplot(data, aes(date, value)) +
  wsj_bands() +                                   # 2011-12 only, with rules = "none"
  geom_col(fill = wsj_pal()(1), width = 25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +                    # the solid zero line
  scale_x_date(labels = wsj_year_label()) +       # 2011 '12 '13
  scale_y_continuous(labels = wsj_label(suffix = "%")) + # the unit on the top label only
  labs(
    title = "Two Words",
    subtitle = "What is measured, in what unit",
    caption = "Source: Who\nThe Wall Street Journal"
  ) +
  theme_wsj(
    paper = "ivory",                              # "gray", with gray type, from August 2013
    subtitle_face = "plain",                      # "bold" until June 2012
    rules = "dotted"                              # "none" with wsj_bands()
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 0))    # labels just after the tick
```

Number callouts are `wsj_callout()`. What the package does not do: the title and text faces (see [Type](#type)), leader-line labels, and the pointer labels, rings, direction arrows, and event markers, which the figure above draws with `annotate()`.

## How this guide was made

**The charts.** The corpus is the set of "native size" graphics (`_NS_` in the file name) that the Internet Archive captured from the *Journal*'s image servers, `si.wsj.net` and `s.wsj.net`, kept if they were flat data graphics in English and checked by hand, `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")` in all. The Asia charts were found first, by a cut on color entropy that kept flat graphics; the U.S. charts later, from the page-one (`P1-`), U.S. news (`NA-`) and Marketplace (`MK-`) file names of 2011 to 2014, each labeled by hand as a chart, a map, a table, or another kind of graphic. Maps and tables are left out. Most Asia charts are 225 pixels wide; the U.S. charts are often larger.

**Readings.** Each Asia chart was read by a Claude subagent, which recorded its text (title, subtitle, notes, source), chart type, labels, callouts, and colors, then read again at twice the size for the rules, ticks, label positions, typefaces, and weights. Where the two readings overlapped they mostly agreed, except on bands: the first reading reported bands on 52 charts that the second saw as dotted rules. A pixel measurement of the band tint decided it for the second reading, and the shares here use it. Two Asia charts that the first pass missed were added later and read once, by eye, at twice the size, with the fields of both readings: `r cite(c("AI-BW445A_SPAIN_NS_20121017130604.jpg", "AI-CI160_AUSTOU_NS_20140424054805.jpg"))`.
The U.S. charts were read once, at twice the size, with the fields of both readings, by eight subagents. They read a sample of `r nrow(us_read)`: every combination of desk and half-year in proportion to its size, at least four charts from each, drawn at random. Each subagent also read three Asia charts that had been read before, 24 in all, so the two sets of readings can be compared. They agreed on the credit line, the axis side, the unit on the top label, the title face, and the line weight of all 24, and on 19 to 23 of 24 for the rules, ticks, label positions, and years. They agreed least on the subtitle weight, 17 of 24, and the new readers called regular subtitles bold: on the larger U.S. charts a regular subtitle looks heavy. A check by eye found the "bold" U.S. subtitles of period C set in the same weight as the regular Asia ones, so the subtitle weights here are the Asia charts' alone, and so, for the same reason, are the line weights.

**Pixel measurements.** Every chart was measured. The field is the modal color of each chart's border. The palette comes from the flat areas of each chart (pixels whose 3-by-3 neighborhood varies by no more than 12 levels, which drops anti-aliased edges and text), binned in CIE Lab and clustered across charts; a chart uses a color if at least 30 of its pixels fall within ΔE 6 of it. Lines are often too thin for this, so a chart's measured colors can miss its lines. The bands are the share of each chart in a tint 2.5 to 12 L* darker than its field.

**Type and labels.** The darkness of the type was measured in each chart's title, subtitle, and source lines, as the darkest 5% of their neutral pixels. A chart has gray type when its subtitle measures gray under a black title. The subtitle decides because the source line is set too small to tell: its letters read as gray on black-type charts too. The second reading's call of the y-label alignment was dropped: on axes whose labels are all one width it took the unit hanging off the top label for left alignment. A by-eye check of 48 Asia charts replaces it.

**Checks.** Every chart cited as an example was looked at, and charts that did not show what was claimed were not cited. The scripts, the readings, and the measurements are kept in a repository of their own, outside the ggthemes source.

**Limits.** Readings of small images miss faint detail: shares of thin features, such as minor ticks, are likely to be low. The corpus is what the Archive happened to capture, so it is not a random sample of the *Journal*'s charts. It has the U.S. desks' web versions of their print graphics, not the printed pages, and no maps or interactive graphics. Shares of the charts read pool a fully read set from the Asia desks with a sample from the larger U.S. desks, so where the two differ this guide gives each.
